segments.say: Imagine a meeting room with a whiteboard and a set of coloured markers. A leader says, no idea is a bad idea, and invites everyone to shout out suggestions. The marker squeaks, the board fills up, and everyone leaves feeling energised. It's one of the most familiar scenes in working life, and a ritual that has been repeated for more than seventy years.

The technique was invented by an advertising executive named Alex Osborn, who described it in his 1953 book Applied Imagination. He proposed four rules: go for quantity, hold back criticism, welcome wild ideas and combine and improve the ideas of others. He claimed that groups using these rules produced far more ideas than they would otherwise.

The idea made perfect sense. If one person has a few ideas, a group of six should have many more, and each idea can spark another. Osborn reported that people in his company's sessions produced many ideas, and the method spread quickly through business, education and government.

For a while, the effectiveness of brainstorming was taken on trust. The groups produced lots of ideas, so it seemed to work. But nobody was asking the more important question. Would the same people have produced more ideas if they'd worked alone? That's the experiment that psychologists eventually ran.

In 1958, Donald Taylor, Paul Berry and Clifford Block at Yale tested Osborn's idea. They compared groups of four people brainstorming together with the same number of individuals working alone. Afterwards, they combined the ideas of the people who had worked alone into what they called nominal groups, which were made up of people who'd never met.

show.what: Does group participation when using brainstorming facilitate or inhibit creative thinking?

segments.say: The nominal groups, made of people working separately, produced roughly twice as many ideas as the real groups, and the ideas were of at least equal quality. In other words, a group of four people working alone, with their results combined, did much better than the same people brainstorming together. It was a shock for the method's fans.

show.title: Result
show.label: the nominal groups produced about twice as many ideas as the real groups

segments.say: That last point is important. People in groups still felt good about the session. They rated the experience as productive and enjoyable. The feeling of success and the measured result had gone in opposite directions.

show.title: What the Yale study found
items: The quality of ideas was no better in groups
People in groups felt that they'd done well

segments.say: Over the following decades, researchers tried to work out why groups did so badly. They found several causes, and they all turned out to be ordinary and human. The first of these is called production blocking.

Michael Diehl and Wolfgang Stroebe tested what was going on, in a series of experiments in Germany. They found that the biggest problem was that only one person can speak at a time. While you're waiting for your turn, you might forget your idea, or decide that it isn't relevant any more, or be distracted by listening to others.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1987
show.what: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: toward the solution of a riddle

segments.say: These are four separate effects. The second is easy to picture. You think of something good, and by the time the person ahead of you has finished, the thought has gone. The third and fourth are very familiar too: evaluation apprehension and social loafing.

show.title: Why group brainstorming loses ideas
items: Only one person can talk at a time
People forget ideas while they wait
Some people hold back for fear of judgement
Some let others do the work

segments.say: Even in a session where criticism is banned, people worry about being judged. They hold back the ideas that feel silly or risky. The no-bad-ideas rule is an attempt to deal with this, but it doesn't fully work, because the fear of looking foolish is not something that a rule can switch off.

There's also the old problem that in groups, effort tends to go down. Bibb Latané and his colleagues had shown in 1979 that people shouted less loudly when they thought they were part of a group. In a brainstorming session, someone who knows that others are contributing may feel less responsible for coming up with ideas.

In 1991, Brian Mullen and colleagues combined twenty studies in a meta-analysis. Their conclusion was blunt. Compared with the same number of people working alone, brainstorming groups produced fewer ideas, in nearly every study, and the more people in the group, the bigger the gap.

show.what: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: a meta-analytic integration

segments.say: So is group brainstorming useless? Not quite. It has social benefits. It can build a sense of team spirit, show everyone that their input is wanted, and help people to learn from each other's views. If the aim is to get everyone on board, a group session may be valuable.

But if the goal is to generate good ideas, the research suggests a better way. Have people think alone first, write down their ideas, and only then bring them together. This approach uses the strengths of both: the freedom of working alone, and the stimulation of seeing others' ideas.

Paul Paulus and Huei-Chuan Yang studied a method called brainwriting, in which people write their ideas on paper and then pass them on for others to build on. Groups that did this produced more ideas than groups who brainstormed aloud, because everyone could think and write at the same time, with no waiting.

show.where: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 2000
show.what: Idea generation in groups: a basis for creativity in organizations

segments.say: It sounds a little less lively than a noisy session at a whiteboard, and that's probably why it's less popular. But the evidence is on its side. It also gives quieter people a fair chance, and stops a single loud voice from setting the direction.

show.title: A recipe that works better
items: Share them anonymously or on paper
Build on each other's ideas in writing

segments.say: You may remember something similar from the first long video, where we saw Asch's experiment, and found that writing down your view before hearing the group made it easier to stay independent. The same principle is at work. Thinking alone first protects the diversity of ideas that a group needs.

It's fair to add that the research is mainly on tasks of idea generation, and that real creative work involves much more than producing a list. It includes choosing, refining and building. Groups are good at some of those. The finding is specific: for sheer quantity of fresh ideas, solo thinking first beats talking in a circle.

An empty room, a whiteboard and a few sticky notes. It's a quiet image of a noisy ritual. The most productive moment may well have been before anyone arrived, when each person sat alone with a pen and a blank page.

It's worth remembering that some of the best ideas in any room are held by the people who say the least. A method that gives everyone time to think and write gives those ideas a chance to be heard. That's good for the results, and it's kinder, too.

So what did we learn? That in 1958, a Yale study found that individuals working alone produced about twice as many ideas as groups. That blocking, fear of judgement and social loafing explain why. That twenty studies agree. And that thinking alone first, then sharing, is a better recipe.

show.sub: What the brainstorming studies taught us

segments.say: Studies of creative teams suggest that the best ones mix solitary and shared work. People think alone, then meet to share and refine, then split up again. They also keep the group diverse, so that different views are heard, and make it safe to disagree. Google's research into its own teams, known as Project Aristotle, found that psychological safety, a shared belief that it's safe to speak up, was the strongest predictor of team success.

The next time you lead a meeting, you might try beginning with five minutes of silence, in which everyone writes down their own ideas. Then go round the room and read them out, one at a time, without comment. It feels strange at first, but it often brings out a wider range of ideas, and it gives everyone, not just the loudest, a first turn.

Where do your own best ideas come from? For many people, the answer is a walk, a shower or a quiet moment alone. Rarely is it a meeting. That fits with what the research says. Good ideas often come when we're relaxed and unobserved, and a group is best used to refine them afterwards, not to produce them on demand under the gaze of colleagues.

Next, we'll look at one of the most famous and most argued-over findings of the last two decades. A two-minute pose that was said to change your hormones, your confidence and even your life, and what happened when other scientists tried to repeat it.
